one_liner: Header-only Grisu2 double-to-string routine; fastest entry in its author's own benchmark, beating std::ostringstream and sprintf().
what_it_does: Header-only C++ function `dtoa_milo(double value, char* buffer)` writes the shortest round-trippable decimal ASCII representation of a double directly into a caller-supplied, null-terminated buffer. It targets the same problem as std::ostringstream/sprintf/std::to_chars (double-to-text formatting) but with a narrower, unsafe C-style interface: no return/error code, no precision control, no NaN/Inf handling, and no documented minimum buffer size. It lives inside the miloyip/dtoa-benchmark harness (src/milo/dtoa_milo.h) rather than being packaged as a standalone library.
how_it_is_fast: Implements Loitsch's Grisu2 algorithm: converts the double into a DiyFp (64-bit significand plus binary exponent), then generates digits using only fixed-width integer/bit arithmetic against a precomputed table of cached powers of ten (GetCachedPower), avoiding the arbitrary-precision bignum fallback that fully-correct converters like Grisu3-based double-conversion sometimes need. A 200-byte two-digit lookup table (GetDigitsLut) speeds up decimal digit and exponent formatting in WriteExponent/Prettify. Being Grisu2 rather than Grisu3, it can occasionally emit a decimal one digit longer than the true shortest representation in exchange for never invoking the slow bignum path.
when_to_use: Hot double-to-ASCII serialization paths (e.g. JSON/log writers) on x86/x86-64 where you control the toolchain (MSVC or GCC/Clang) and can vendor a single header.
You've already excluded NaN/Inf upstream and can size and validate the output buffer yourself.

You want the fastest Grisu-family converter shown in this specific benchmark and are willing to re-benchmark it against double-conversion/fpconv on your own hardware and compiler rather than trust the 2013-era, i7-920/VC2013 numbers.
'Almost always shortest' output (not the guaranteed-shortest of Grisu3+bignum) is acceptable for your format.
when_not_to_use: You need a std::to_chars-compatible signature (pointer-pair/span, error code, format flags) — this is a raw C-style buffer writer, not drop-in.
You need guaranteed-correct NaN/Inf handling — the code only asserts !isnan/!isinf, which is compiled out under NDEBUG (undefined behavior in release).

Your value distribution can hit the known unresolved out-of-bounds read in DigitGen (e.g. 0.020000000000000005, kappa = -14) — GitHub issue #7, filed 2016, still open as of 2026-09-24, caught by Clang ASan, no fix landed in this repo.

You need an actively maintained dependency — repo has had no default-branch commits since 2020-04-27, and issue #18 explicitly asks the maintainer to transfer ownership because he isn't accepting pull requests.

Target is a non-x86 platform — the fast paths use MSVC's _umul128/_BitScanReverse64 or GCC/Clang's __int128/__builtin_clzll on x86-64; other architectures fall back to an untested, unbenchmarked portable path.

integration.form: header-only (source-drop from a benchmark repo; not distributed as a standalone package — must be extracted from src/milo/dtoa_milo.h)
integration.dependencies: none beyond the C/C++ standard library (assert.h, math.h, stdint.h); on MSVC it also pulls in a bundled msinttypes/stdint.h shim and <intrin.h>
integration.min_toolchain: not documented; the source itself only requires C++03-level syntax plus compiler intrinsics/extensions (MSVC any version with _umul128/_BitScanReverse64; GCC >=4.6 or Clang for __int128 on x86-64); portable fallback compiles with any C++ compiler
integration.platforms: x86-64 optimized via MSVC or GCC/Clang intrinsics; portable C++ fallback for other compilers/architectures exists in source but is not covered by the published benchmark numbers
integration.thread_safety: not documented; implementation holds no mutable global state (only function-local static const lookup tables) and writes only to the caller-provided buffer, so concurrent calls with distinct buffers appear safe, but this is not asserted by the author
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — different signature (raw buffer write, no error code, no precision/format control, no NaN/Inf handling) than std::ostringstream or std::to_chars; needs a wrapper to substitute at call sites

gotchas: Open, unresolved bug (issue #7, filed 2016): certain values, e.g. 0.020000000000000005, cause an out-of-bounds read on the internal kPow10 table inside DigitGen (kappa = -14), caught by Clang AddressSanitizer.
assert(!isnan(value)); assert(!isinf(value)) — with NDEBUG (release builds) these are no-ops, so NaN/Inf input is undefined behavior rather than a checked error.
No buffer-size parameter or internal bound check; caller must supply a sufficiently large buffer with no guidance from the header on how large that needs to be.

Issue #20 (wrong result for 16385.0, a rounding-direction bug in the cached-power exponent calculation) was fixed by the maintainer, closed on the same date as the repo's last commit (2020-04-27) — confirms the currently-read source no longer has that specific bug, but shows fixes were rare and reactive.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Against fpconv (also Grisu2, 4.59x vs sprintf) and google/double-conversion (Grisu3+bignum fallback, 6.23x, always-shortest), milo is the fastest of the three on this same benchmark/hardware (9.10x vs sprintf) but carries the same Grisu2 not-always-shortest caveat as fpconv plus an unresolved OOB read that neither sibling has documented against it; pick milo only after your own benchmark confirms the throughput edge and you can tolerate or patch the DigitGen edge case, otherwise prefer double-conversion (more correctness testing, used in V8) or Boost.Charconv/c4core (independently benchmarked, actively maintained, std::to_chars-compatible APIs).
verified_claims_summary: On the benchmark's own RandomDigit case (1,000 random doubles with 1-17 significant decimal digits, minimum of 10 trials x 100 iterations each), milo averaged 138.021 ns/conversion versus sprintf's 1256.376 ns (9.10x, the page's own figure) and versus std::ostringstream's 2,778.748 ns (~20.1x, derived from the same table), measured on an Intel Core i7 920 @ 2.67GHz with Visual C++ 2013, Windows 64-bit, release config.
status_note: Abandoned: no default-branch commits since 2020-04-27, and an open issue (#18) asks the maintainer to transfer ownership since he no longer accepts pull requests; MIT-licensed and small enough to vendor as a single header, but ships with at least one known, unresolved memory-safety bug (issue #7) that has sat open since 2016.
